title: RBA flags AI role in changing the job market
full_text:
The Reserve Bank of Australia says there are signs the growth of artificial intelligence use is beginning to seep into the jobs market, with early indications that younger workers are among the most exposed.
While there was little evidence of widespread disruption so far, the central bank's research suggested an exponential increase in job advertisements containing AI-related terminology since the launch of OpenAI's popular ChatGPT platform kick-started a surge in the technology's use.
"Like other major technological shifts, AI is likely to change the job market significantly," said RBA chief economist Sarah Hunter in a speech in Sydney on Monday that she acknowledged was drafted using AI.
She said the central bank was conscious that headline labour data could "mask disruptive displacement effects" in particular areas.
"There are tentative signs of adjustment, through weaker job ad posting and employment outcomes in more AI-exposed occupations, and stronger growth in areas where the technology has had less of an impact, particularly for younger workers," Hunter told the UBS Australasia Conference.
Those comments were supported by new research published by the RBA that pointed to signs of disruption in industries particularly exposed to AI automation - such as software development, clerical work and administration - as well as younger workers.
"AI adoption could have material implications for the labour market, although the timing, scale and direction of any future impacts are highly uncertain," wrote Mike Major, a manager in the bank's economic analysis department.
Major's research showed the share of job advertisements containing AI-related technology had surged exponentially since ChatGPT's release four years ago, and that job postings in AI-exposed sectors had slowed more than for other occupations.
Hunter said the growth in the use and sophistication of AI was likely to have more complicated effects on employment than job losses.
In her speech, she cited research that estimated 4 per cent of workers were highly exposed to job automation, while 31 per cent were exposed to having part of their work complemented or augmented by AI processes.
High-profile job cuts at National Australia Bank and design software giant Canva have raised fears of a retrenchment spike in recent weeks, with Australia on track for its highest number of redundancies since the pandemic.
The RBA's research accords with findings from other central banks and similar bodies. The International Monetary Fund has estimated about 60 per cent of jobs in advanced economies are exposed to AI disruption.
US Federal Reserve research published in September showed the share of workers worried about losing their job to AI had more than doubled in just a year.
Hunter said whatever the impact on the labour market, the transition would not result in continual "downward pressure on inflation", with extra supply capacity in the economy generated by the technology likely to be met by growing demand. She also warned that the benefits of AI were "unlikely to be distributed evenly".
"Some workers may face a difficult period of adjustment as demand for particular roles or tasks decline, which will weigh on income and spending by some households," she said.
"The strength of the consumption response will depend not only on the overall increase in income, but also on how broadly the gains are shared across the economy and the pathway for integrating the technology into our daily lives."
The RBA estimates that about 5.3 per cent of household financial wealth was exposed to AI-related equities, either directly or through superannuation, more than double the 2 per cent expected four years ago.
